title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

reading.body:
An AI system generated a fabricated news article depicting a Reserve Bank Governor storming out of an interview with a finance presenter over a cryptocurrency platform. The interview never occurred. The false article was designed to build credibility for an investment scam, part of a broader pattern where AI is used to impersonate well-known Australians in fraudulent schemes.

This is a deployment failure of AI as an impersonation tool. The system was used outside any legitimate purpose to create convincing false content at scale. A human check—verification that the interview happened, or that the supposed source organization had published it—would have stopped the scam before victims encountered it. It is not established whether the scammers built or merely used existing generative AI systems.

The broader problem is not with the AI systems themselves but with how they have been deployed as components in fraud operations. The systems generate content that appears authentic enough to deceive people about the endorsements and statements of real figures, enabling scammers to collect personal information and money from victims.

reports.title: The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise
AI deepfake scams 'an emergency in the making' as ASIC reports rise in false investment endorsements
ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

summary:
A fake online article depicted Reserve Bank Governor Michele Bullock storming out of an interview with ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler over questions about Boulder Sparhaven, an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform. The interview never actually occurred. This fabricated story represents a growing category of scam that uses artificial intelligence to create convincing but false content featuring well-known Australians. The Australian Securities and Investments Commission reports that such AI-generated investment scams are becoming increasingly prevalent and sophisticated.

ASIC's latest research reveals alarming growth in investment fraud, with the regulator removing 19,400 scams last year, a 182 percent increase. Phishing scams jumped 279 percent, while fake investment platforms rose 151 percent. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese tops the list of impersonated figures, followed by other politicians and financial personalities including Alan Kohler, who is among the most commonly targeted. Scammers create elaborate deceptions by building fake websites, news articles, and social media presence to establish credibility before requesting personal information or money from victims.
